intuition: A negative number can turn the smallest negative product into the largest positive product. For that reason, save both the smallest and largest products ending at each position. For the next value, compare starting fresh with extending each of those two products.

Track high and low for nonempty subarrays ending at the current position. Every next ending subarray either starts fresh at the current value or extends an old ending subarray. Compare the current value with its products against both old extremes, then choose a new maximum and minimum. Zero automatically makes both products zero and permits a later fresh start.

The old extremes must be read together before either is overwritten. Updating high and then using that new value to compute low would accidentally apply the current factor twice. The global best is separate: an earlier ending subarray may remain best possible after later negatives or zeros arrive.
Initializing all three values from nums[0] respects the requirement that the selected subarray is nonempty.

steps: At 3, candidates are 3 and 6. Set high=6, low=3, best=6.
At -2, candidates are -2, -12, and -6. Set high=-2 and low=-12.
The global best remains 6 even though the current ending maximum is negative.
At 4, candidates are 4, -8, and -48. Set high=4 and low=-48.
Return best=6, the product of the earlier contiguous subarray [2,3].

codeNotes.note: Both transitions need the previous position’s extremes, not one partially updated value.

codeNotes.code: high = max(value, value * old_high, value * old_low)
codeNotes.note: Allow starting fresh and both sign-sensitive extensions.
An earlier subarray can remain best possible even when the current ending product worsens.

keyDecision: Compute both new extremes from the old extremes before updating either saved value.

concept.question: Why might the worst negative product become tomorrow’s best positive product?
intuition: Remembering only the greatest product ending here loses useful negative history. Multiplying by another negative can reverse the order of best and worst candidates.

Keep both the greatest and least products ending at the current position. The next value may start fresh, extend the greatest, or extend the least. Compare all three and retain both new extremes, plus the historical greatest product.
concept.observation: Use both previous extremes when multiplying by the next value.
approach: Initialize both ending extremes from the first value.
Compare starting fresh with extending each previous extreme.
Update both extremes and the historical maximum.
concept.correctness: Every section ending at a new value either starts there or extends a previous ending section. A positive multiplier preserves product order and a negative reverses it, so the prior greatest and least products cover both possibilities. Comparing those extensions and a restart gives exact new extremes. The greatest historical ending product is the overall answer.

complexity.explanation: Three candidate products per value give linear work. Two ending extremes and one historical answer use constant extra memory.

pitfalls: Remember the least product as well as the greatest.
Compute new extremes from the previous extremes.
Handle zero and all-negative inputs without an empty section.

illustrations.caption: A negative factor can turn the least product into the greatest. Keep both extremes before extending to the next position.

scenes.title: A positive extension wins
scenes.narration: For [2,3,-2,4], after 3 the greatest ending product is 6 and the least is 3.
scenes.decision: A section can restart at the current value.

scenes.title: A negative reverses the extremes
scenes.narration: With -2, candidates are -2, -12, and -6. The greatest ending product is -2 and least -12.
scenes.decision: Multiplication by a negative reverses product ordering.

scenes.title: The earlier maximum survives
scenes.narration: With 4, candidates are 4,-8,-48. The ending greatest is 4, but the earlier [2,3] product 6 remains the answer.
scenes.decision: Historical maximum and current ending maximum differ.

scenes.title: Why the answer is complete

A positive multiplier preserves product order and a negative reverses it, so the prior greatest and least products cover both possibilities. Comparing those extensions and a restart gives exact new extremes. The greatest historical ending product is the overall answer.

scenes.title: A boundary to remember
scenes.narration: A zero ends any nonzero product crossing it, but later sections may restart.
scenes.decision: Do not allow an earlier zero to prevent a future positive answer.
